sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section raises questions about the verse "And these are the judgments," noting the grammatical shift from plural to singular and the Jerusalem Talmud's interpretation of "tashim" as hidden treasure, and asks why the laws begin with a Hebrew slave.

translations.translation: "And these are the judgments which you shall place before them: When you acquire a Hebrew slave, etc."
And the precise point in this is known,
that "before them" is plural and third person, while "you shall acquire" is singular and second person.
Also, one must understand what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud
on the verse "And these are the judgments which you shall place before them,"
that "tashim" (you shall place) is from the term "simah"
(a treasure)
that is not revealed, etc.,
the secrets of the Torah.
And it needs to be understood,
for judgments are the laws that are also understood by human intellect
[and even by the intellect of the nations of the world],
and what is the connection of judgments to "tashim" from the term "simah,"
the secrets of the Torah?
Also, one must understand
why the judgments begin with the law of a Hebrew slave.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the Hebrew slave spiritually represents serving G-d with acceptance of the yoke, and that even intellectually understood commandments must be performed with this servant-like devotion, as their essence is G-d's super-rational will.

translations.translation: Now, it is explained in Ohr HaTorah,
that the concept of a Hebrew slave in spirituality is,
that his service of G-d is in a manner of acceptance of the yoke,
the service of a servant.
And based on this, it can be said,
that the fact that the judgments begin with the law of a Hebrew slave,
is to hint,
that even the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments,
which are understood by the intellect,
must be performed from the aspect of acceptance of the yoke,
in the manner of the service of a servant.
For although from the fact that these commandments are called in the Torah of Truth by the name "judgments," it is understood that these commandments must also be fulfilled from the aspect of reason,
nevertheless,
the essence of their fulfillment must be in a manner of acceptance of the yoke,
both from the aspect of the person fulfilling the commandments,
that his fulfillment of the commandments must be in a manner of the service of a servant,
and also from the aspect of the commandments,
for all the commandments
(even the commandments of judgments)
their essence is that they are the will of the Holy One, blessed be He,
a will that is above reason,
except that the Holy One, blessed be He, decreed that the will of these commandments should also be clothed in reason.
And to add,
that this—that even the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments must be in a manner of acceptance of the yoke—
is also in the matter of the judgments within them.

That is, that these commandments must also be fulfilled from the aspect of reason is because such is the command of the Holy One, blessed be He, that the fulfillment of these commandments should also be from the aspect of reason.
And it can be said,
that this is what our sages, of blessed memory, said
on the verse "And these are the judgments,"
"And these" adds to the first ones,
just as the first ones were from Sinai, so too these are from Sinai,
for at the giving of the Torah
(Sinai)
the Jewish people became servants to the Holy One, blessed be He,
and the hint of "so too these are from Sinai" is,
that even the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments,
including also this matter that they must be fulfilled also from the aspect of reason
[so too these,
judgments],
must be in a manner of the service of a servant.
And therefore the judgments begin with the law of a Hebrew slave,
in order to hint,
that even the commandments of judgments,
the primary approach
(the first approach)
to their study and fulfillment is acceptance of the yoke,
the service of a servant.
And a further explanation,
that since the essence of servitude is in a Canaanite slave
[for in addition to the fact that a Hebrew slave serves only six years
(and also a slave with a bored ear goes out in the Jubilee)
and regarding a Canaanite slave it is written,
"You shall work with them forever,"
the subjugation
(the servitude)
of a Hebrew slave
(even when he is a slave)
is not like the subjugation
(servitude)
of a Canaanite slave],
therefore, in order to hint at the above concept
(that the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments must be in a manner of the service of a servant)
it would seemingly have been necessary for the judgments to begin with the law of a Canaanite slave.
